about: The first-party modules the bundler keeps for their side effects alone (#27's Architecture, #300): treeshake.moduleSideEffects is true only for each pass's entry roots and these, so any other module nothing takes anything from drops whole (scripts/build/bundle.js's sideEffectsFor). A first-party import made for side effects only, import './x.js', has to name a module here, or the build fails as side-effects/unlisted, since the bundler would drop it unseen. Each group names the issue that owns its modules and why they run for their side effects. The list only shrinks: a module no such import names fails as side-effects/stale, and test/build-side-effects.test.js pins what it may hold. A list that doesn't read fails as side-effects/file (scripts/build/side-effects.js).

groups.reason: The new tab's legacy graph, which js/main.js imports for side effects alone, in the order it runs: each legacy file sets up its global (window.Utils, window.Storage and the rest) when it runs, and the others read those globals. Its two composition modules, block-projections.js and rendering.js, are #14's ports the legacy scripts read blocks and render rich text through, so they leave with the legacy graph. #3's rebuilt Workspace retires the graph.

The network guard's installer, which js/network-guard.js and the indexer's module worker import for side effects alone. It wraps every network API the guard covers when it runs, so it has to run before any other import.
